books.section: Topic 4.13 The Society of the South in the Early Republic, A. Slavery and the Southern “Way of Life”

primary_sources: Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832, 1832

stimulus.text:
After Nat Turner's rebellion in Southampton County, Virginia, in August 1831, the Virginia legislature debated ending slavery in the winter of 1831-1832. The debate failed, and Thomas R. Dew, a professor at the College of William and Mary, defended slavery in a pamphlet published in 1832:

“In the debate in the Virginia legislature, no speaker insinuated even, we believe that the slaves in Virginia were not treated kindly; and all too agreed that they were most abundantly fed, and we have no doubt but that they form the happiest portion of our society.”

“A merrier being does not exist on the face of the globe than the negro slave of the United States.”
stimulus.source_note: Quotations verbatim from Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832 (1832), p. 66, as quoted in the Contemporary Argumentation and Debate account of Dew's pamphlet and in the Free Library account. Context checked against Digital History, University of Houston (ID 370).

source: original; stimulus verbatim from Thomas R. Dew, Review of the Debate in the Virginia Legislature of 1831 and 1832 (1832), public domain
stem: Dew's pamphlet and the failure of the Virginia debate best show which change in the South after 1831?

options.text: Southern legislatures began freeing enslaved people gradually
options.misconception: The Virginia debate failed; no Southern legislature began gradual emancipation after 1831.

options.text: Virginia became the first Southern state to abolish slavery
options.misconception: Virginia kept slavery; the debate ended with slavery still in place.

options.text: The defense of slavery hardened from apology into open praise
Southern planters stopped growing cotton and turned to factories
options.misconception: Planters grew more cotton after 1831, and the South built few factories.

rationales.A: The Virginia debate failed. No Southern legislature began gradual emancipation after 1831.
rationales.B: Virginia kept slavery. The debate ended with slavery still in place.
rationales.C: Virginia debated ending slavery and kept it, and Dew answered by calling enslaved people the happiest part of society. Apology had become praise.
rationales.D: Planters grew more cotton after 1831, and the South built few factories.
rationales.general:
1. Note what happened. Virginia openly debated ending slavery, then voted to keep it.
2. Read Dew. He does not excuse slavery as a sad need; he calls enslaved people the happiest part of society.
3. Name the shift. The old defense called slavery a necessary evil, and the new defense called it good.
Background: After Turner, Southern states also tightened their slave codes instead of loosening them.
Remember: when a reform fails, watch how its opponents change their argument.
